newsitem.title: USA: No meeting yet to plan presidential debates.
newsitem.headline: No meeting yet to plan presidential debates.

text.p: The first presidential debate is just three weeks away, but the campaigns of President Bill Clinton and Bob Dole cannot even agree on how to discuss the format and it's unclear whether Ross Perot will take part.

Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart said on Tuesday the Democrats were not ready to meet with Dole's Republicans and work on the details of the televised debates, the first of which is tentatively scheduled for Sept. 25 in St. Louis.

Dole campaign officials wrote to their Clinton counterparts last week asking for a debate planning meeting. But Lockhart said it seemed the Republicans were trying to keep Perot, the Texas billionaire and Reform Party presidential candidate, out of the planning.

"I think if you look closely at what they're saying, that's exactly what they are trying to do (cut out Perot)," Lockhart told Reuters. "They have said they don't really think Perot should be involved in the debates."

Lockhart also accused the Dole campaign of trying to sideline the Commission on Presidential Debates, which sponsored the forums in 1988 and 1992 and will determine by mid-September whether Perot can participate this year.
"I don't think at this point we're ready to set up a meeting (with the Dole campaign)," Lockhart said. "We're looking forward to discussing the debates with the commission."
Perot participated in the 1992 presidential debates as an independent candidate. Since then he has converted his United We Stand movement into a national party, the Reform Party.
But prominent Republicans have said they fear Perot will draw more votes from Dole than Clinton, and the televised debates are the most-watched events of the campaign.
The final debate of 1992 between then-President George Bush, Clinton and Perot drew a record debate audience of 97 million -- more than one in three Americans.
Dole campaign spokeswoman Christina Martin denied the Republicans were trying to keep Perot out of the debates, or undermine the Commission on Presidential Debates.
"The commission traditionally makes recommendations and we look forward to their input, but we also look forward to sitting down and negotiating with the (Clinton) campaign," Martin said.

The Dole campaign communication's director, John Buckley, said earlier this week the Republicans have a "real question" about whether Perot should share the debate stage, noting he is one of several third party candidates.
But the Perot campaign expects he will share the debate spotlight again this year, said spokeswoman Sharon Holman.

"I think there is no way to deny Perot a spot at the table, when he's getting federal matching funds, he will be on the ballot in all 50 states and he won 19 percent of the vote in the 1992 election," Holman said.

Perot's support in the polls is currently running at about 6 to 8 percent. Clinton appears to have overcome the bounce Dole got after the recent Republican convention, and the president has moved back to a 15 to 20 percent lead over Dole.
In addition to Sept. 25, the commission has proposed two other presidential debates on Oct. 9 and Oct. 16, as well as a vice presidential debate on Oct. 2.
